The post How Online Fandom Is Rewriting the IP Playbook appeared first on Naavik .
text:
Backrooms | Source: A24 Pictures
“People don’t want to just watch anymore. They want to participate,” says Cathy Hackl , describing the future of new IP. She’s pointing at a telling 2026: Netflix’s upcoming Unhinged turns your phone into a controller — flashlight, receiver of in-game calls and texts — while A24’s Backrooms became the studio’s biggest film based on a world its audience had spent years exploring through YouTube videos and games.
Hollywood has always mined other media for its next franchise: comic books (Marvel, Batman), toy lines like Transformers ($5.4B worldwide box office), and video games from Angry Birds ($352M) to Super Mario ($1.36B) to Minecraft ($960M).
The stranger story is on the internet's darker fringe, where horror memes and Gen Z/Alpha "nonsense" are finding their way to Hollywood, oddly, in part through gaming. Slender Man and Five Nights at Freddy's teed this up in years past, with 2026's Backrooms as the latest breakout example. However, what’s interesting and novel about Backrooms is that the IP started as a meme and grew organically through countless creators, until a next-generation standout creator ultimately took it to the next level. Is this a new playbook for the future of emergent, internet-native IP? Let’s break it down.
Checking Into the Backrooms
Backrooms | Source: A24 Pictures
The Backrooms began in May 2019 as an anonymous 4chan post : a grainy photo of an empty, yellow-carpeted office under buzzing fluorescent lights — with the idea that you could "noclip" out of reality (a gaming term for clipping through a wall) into an endless maze of rooms stalked by entities, with no way out. It became part of the "creepypasta" category — user-generated internet horror folklore that anyone can copy, remix, and extend.
Apeirophobia | Source: Polaroid Studios, Roblox
In January 2022, 16-year-old Kane Parsons turned it into a Blair Witch-style YouTube series that drew tens of millions of views. In parallel, creators built hundreds of Backrooms games on Steam and Roblox; the biggest by user count, Apeirophobia, has over 422 million visits on Roblox. Then Hollywood called: A24 optioned Parsons' shorts in February 2023 and released the film in May 2026 to roughly $330 million worldwide on a sub-$10 million budget, A24's biggest launch ever, with Parsons, at 20, the youngest director to top the U.S. box office.
Temporary uplift in Apeirophobia CCU around movie launch | Source: Creator Exchange
Would A24 have optioned an unsettling photo off 4chan? Of course not. What it bet on was Parsons: a singular, internet-native talent with a proven ability to create for a large audience. But the fandom he tapped into was bigger than any single YouTube channel — or even YouTube itself. Gen Z and Gen Alpha had already walked the Backrooms on Roblox, and the hundreds of millions of gameplay visits kept the world alive between videos, helping the film become a far larger sensation than it may have otherwise been. Digital-native IPs build fandom momentum across platforms, and Roblox in particular is starting to play a role on par with YouTube.
Horrific Recipes for Success
From Slender Man to Backrooms, it has mostly been horror that makes the jump from meme to game to Hollywood. A successful horror concept has a vibe, lore, and rules rather than a fixed character and plot, so anyone can build and remix their own take. It is a more cost-efficient genre to produce for both games and films. The same shareability that spreads a scary meme makes jump-scare reaction videos endlessly rewatchable.
Slender: The Arrival | Source: Blue Isle Publishing
Slender Man, a faceless figure in a dark suit invented by Eric Knudson in 2009 as a submission on the Something Awful forums, went viral through multiple independently developed games (notably SlenderMan: The Arrival and Slender: The Eight Pages ) and reaction videos from PewDiePie and Markiplier . It then reached a 2018 Sony film (~$52M on a ~$10M budget, panned at 8% on Rotten Tomatoes ). It was arguably the first meme to run the full route: forum post to fan-made games to Hollywood.
Five Nights at Freddy's | Source: Scott Cawthorn
Five Nights at Freddy' s ran the loop in the other direction: Scott Cawthon built it in 2014 as a low-budget indie game that itself spawned memes and theories through Let's Play footage, grew into a cross-platform hit, and seeded two Blumhouse films that grossed over $500M combined.
What’s notable is that games, memes, and video content increasingly feed one another as the foundation for what becomes popular in today’s online ecosystem. Decentralized fandom builds organic growth — even when the IP isn’t owned by anyone — while standout talent helps take it to the next level.
99 Nights in the Forest | Source: Grandma’s Favorite Games, Roblox
We continue to see echoes of this pattern in Roblox breakout 99 Nights in the Forest . After amassing 26 billion visits and reaching an all-time peak of 14.2 million concurrent players , the game sparked a competitive bidding war for its film rights, which 20th Century Studios ultimately won . All three of the game's creators signed on as executive producers. Mob Entertainment’s Poppy Playtime — a similar example that began on Steam before blossoming into physical toys and a plethora of Roblox experiences — recently closed a movie deal with Legendary , the producers behind the Five Nights at Freddy's films. In these cases, there is a clear owner of the IP, whether talent on par with Parsons can help them succeed on the big screen remains an open question.
Skibidi Toilet | Source: Gerasimov, Invisible Narratives
We are also beginning to see examples beyond horror and more in the emerging “brainrot” category that took Gen Alpha by storm. Skibidi Toilet, which began in 2023 as YouTube videos about a war between toilets and "cameramen," racked up 47 million subscribers and 20 billion views . It also experienced an explosion of Skibidi-inspired Roblox games (like Toilet Tower Defense, which passed 6.1 billion visits ), leading to its movie rights getting scooped up. Steal a Brainrot — the Roblox experience in which players collect and steal bizarre characters from one another, now up to 70.8 billion visits — got optioned by Story Kitchen . Its source material draws from a meme-driven IP with diffuse, largely open ownership . Of course, optioned movies don’t always make it to the finish line, and we’ll see if they do as the popularity of these IPs lose momentum online (what rises fastest often fades quickly too).
Who Do You Meme?
Halloween promo | Source: Roblox
When a community develops the IP, ownership becomes the sticking point on the road to Hollywood. You can option a creator, but you cannot option a meme.
Slender Man had one identifiable creator, and a film got made. The SCP Foundation , a collaborative-horror wiki from 2007, spun off games whose biggest Roblox entry has over 800 million visits but, tellingly, no film. Backrooms sits in between: A24 couldn't buy the concept, because no one owns the original idea, so it signed Kane Parsons directly and adapted the characters and ideas he contributed to the open IP.
Then there is the platform itself. Roblox owns the platform but not the worlds on it: creators keep their copyright and sell freely. Roblox takes a large cut of on-platform spending — it paid creators over $1 billion last year — and asserts no claim on the IP itself. Like YouTube, Roblox is where culture spreads: memes and ideas inspire creators, creators build worlds, these worlds expand the fan base, and fans deepen the IP.
Related, a UGC platform does three jobs no marketing department can: It hands world-building over to thousands of creators (sometimes for free), enables converting videos fans watch into worlds they play in, and it produces live demand signals (visits and concurrents) that are often more telling than a trailer view count. As a result, “user generated fandom” becomes an organic, growing force that elevates simple memes or IP into deep, lore-filled worlds that millions of people become interested in, setting the foundation for even more creation and success to come.
Something Wicked This Way Comes
Freaky Nikki from Obsession | Source: Focus Features
It isn't only a gaming phenomenon, either: Hollywood increasingly wants a proven crowd before acquiring adaptation rights, the way the music industry now expects a following before it signs. Self-published novelist Matt Dinniman's Dungeon Crawler Carl grew organically enough to secure a Peacock series; TikTok comedian Curry Barker's channel @thatsabadidea attracted funding for Obsession , another summer indie breakout, grossing over $370 million against a $750,000 budget.
A layer of specialists is also forming in between creators and the industry. On Naavik's podcast , Story Kitchen’s co-founder Dmitri Johnson, who optioned Steal a Brainrot, compared the moment to the early, dismissed days of YouTube and encourages peers to engage these worlds without strip-mining them (think of Hollywood’s push to acquire any and all comic book IP in the ‘90s/’00s).
Of course, adaptations can be slow. A24 optioned Backrooms in early 2023 and released it three years later (fast, by Hollywood standards), so the options now in development will take years to prove out, if ever. The pipeline is unforgiving: most meme-to-film attempts land poorly even when they turn a profit, hyped memes and IP can flame out before a film is ready, and it takes judgment to know what will last: being ubiquitous is not the same as being good.
A handful of Backrooms-inspired Roblox experiences | Source: Roblox
If we pierce through all the noise, what’s really emerging is a new kind of IP development process. Internet-native IP may have a single spark (like the Backrooms meme on 4chan), but it’s increasingly owned by the collective. Platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and Roblox are the cultural petri dishes in which the network effect of millions of creators and fans bring the IP universes to life in an organic, compounding way. Out of these passionate creators occasionally comes an internet-native, next-generation elite talent (like Parsons) that can transcend the crowd and take an IP to new heights in new ways.
Not all internet-native IP will have the same story, so we shouldn’t extrapolate from Backrooms too heavily, but we expect to see more echoes of this type of IP growth in the years to come. For the games industry, it’s worth double-underlining that Roblox, in particular, is a cultural vessel for upcoming generations more so than any other platform. So the next time a kid or teenager yells “six-seven,” “Skibidi,” or whatever new goofy phrase at you, remember: it might be coming, soon, to a screen near you.

Xbox, Amazon and Netflix try to make game streaming relevant – The Game Business Micro
This week, we dive into Xbox’s new ad experiment and chat about the role of game streaming in the current climate
Christopher Dring
Jul 27, 2026
∙ Paid
Happy Monday!
Sometimes, when someone calls me a ‘video game journalist’, I will correct them. I’ll say, ‘well, more a video game business journalist’.
This isn’t because of some snobbery towards games journalism. It’s because after 20 years of doing this exact job, my brain has become twisted by it. Even when a game I love gets announced – like Resident Evil Veronica or the new Ocarina of Time remake - I’m immediately analysing commercial potential, the competitor landscape, distribution strategies… rather than gameplay features. I can’t help it. It’s a curse
And it’s not always to my benefit. Take last week’s interview with Amazon. In that interview, the company let slip that Tomb Raider Catalyst is scheduled for launch in 2028. The game was previously announced for 2027. I noticed it immediately. But I also didn’t feel it was much of a story. The game had a vague date anyway. It isn’t impacting TGB readers, is it? And is it a surprise? The Tomb Raider remake (Legacy of Atlantis) had been delayed out of 2026 and into 2027… and that likely had some impact on the next game. Does Amazon really want two Tomb Raiders in one year?
So, I didn’t run a story on it. It’s not even referenced in the newsletter. It’s a very brief, off-hand moment in a podcast. But, of course, the consumer media did spot it. And soon there were stories on all major websites about the Tomb Raider delay.
There’s a part of me that’s annoyed with myself. How much traffic did I miss out on by not running that as a standalone story? But then, that’s not what The Game Business is all about. I guess it’s nice that folk are paying that much attention.
The stories that got me most excited last week were all around game streaming. The Amazon chat was about its ambitions for its game streaming platform Luna, which can now be found within the Prime Video app. And just hours after that went out, Xbox announced it was experimenting with a new advertising-based business model related to its own streaming service.
So, let’s talk about that, shall we!
Can Xbox’s big advertising experiment make game streaming work this time?
In Brief: Xbox is testing a new business model for game streaming, where players can stream their game library for free with ads. The two-minutes of ads will appear before the game starts and run every hour. Previously, game streaming was limited to Xbox Game Pass subscribers.
What You Need To Know:
This test is for Xbox Insiders and is very much an experiment.
The premium subscription option via Game Pass remains.
The ads won’t interrupt gameplay, but sessions are limited to one hour in length.
The firm insists the ads should ‘create value’ and will be held to ‘the same quality bar as the content’.
Xbox Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball is intrigued by the advertising business model. He spoke with us about it in February before he joined Microsoft. We discussed it again after he joined last month.
In other game streaming news, Amazon has added its Luna streaming service to the Prime Video app. Now Prime members can stream games directly through Prime Video.
Both moves follow the launch of two big streaming games from Netflix: The horror story game Unhinged and the FIFA World Cup game.
My Take:
Occasionally you get moments where a bunch of similar(ish) stories come along at the same time.
Two weeks ago, we featured Netflix after it launched game streaming horror hit Unhinged. Then shortly after, Amazon popped in to announce it is further integrating its Luna game streaming platform into Prime Video. And just hours after that, Xbox announced it is experimenting with pre-roll ads for its own game streaming service.
Streaming is back in the conversation right now. But the big questions remain unanswered. Could it unlock new players and help video games with its growth problem? Can it offer a viable alternative for people who have been priced out of consoles?
Regular readers/listeners of The Game Business will have heard me say that ‘the things that will get video games back to growth are video games’. It’s not a distribution model, or a new form of monetization, or a new technology. You can have the best business strategy, but it amounts to nothing if you don’t have a hit game. And equally, you can have a questionable got-to-market plan, but that can be overcome by a special game or two (which is pretty much the story of Nintendo).
In my view, game streaming will only take off if there are games that people want to experience via it.
But these are unprecedented times. The rapidly rising cost of hardware components and the volatile political landscape, threatens the foundations of the industry (certainly the PC and console industry). What if gamers can’t afford the next consoles? Or can’t upgrade their gaming PCs?
I’m not convinced even a special game can persuade a large audience to buy a $1,000 PlayStation 6.

title: How Toon Blast Became the Best Business in Puzzle
author: Aylin Yazıcı
excerpt:
How did Toon Blast grow its ARPDAU while every other blast game was falling
off a cliff?
text:
Written by Aylin , your former Puzzle Addict & Consultant at Deconstructor of Fun
This month's Puzzly Monthly episode went back in time to answer a listener question that turned into something bigger: how did Toon Blast grow its ARPDAU while every other blast game was falling off a cliff?
The answer covers a decade of genre history, one very fast feature copy, and a live-ops rebuild that most people are still crediting to the wrong thing.
Make sure to watch the episode for the full discussion.
Blast broke the puzzle rules on purpose
Before Toy Blast, "blast" wasn't a genre. It was clicker-match, and the closest reference points were Pet Rescue Saga and Diamond Digger: scrolling boards, a single correct solve path, and a fail rate baked into the design. The episode digs up a detail about Pet Rescue's early funnel, which is that its success curve went down before it went up, because players needed a few attempts to work out the right answer before they could solve it consistently. That friction was considered a bug at the time, and teams were actively trying to engineer it out. Today the same design sits at the heart of Block Jam and the whole solitaire-association wave, where failing three times before you crack a board is the product.
Diamond Digger gameplay on the left, Pet Rescue Saga on the right
Toy Blast took the clicker-match core and made it feel like Candy Crush instead. Solid screen, no scrolling, blockers and boosters that stay on the board, more luck, less strategy. Toon Blast went further and shipped without a saga map at a point where you effectively could not launch a casual game without one, and put everything into gameplay and events.
The instinct in this industry is always to add: more structure, more progression, more correct answers that reward mastery. Blast won by subtracting. Strip out the meta layer and the mental strategy, and what's left is closer to a slot pull than a puzzle. That's why blast early and mid retention has never looked like the rest of the category, and it's the part most teams still get backwards when they try to compete on depth.
Everyone was fighting over Match-3 and left the door open
Here's the part that should sting if you were scoping games in 2014: nobody went after clickers on purpose. Match-3 was the prize, bubble shooters were second, and clickers were the genre nobody felt threatened by, because the assumption was that it just wasn't a big enough market to matter.
Peak went after third place and did it properly, and has since crossed $5 billion in user spending, with Toon Blast accounting for around 60% of it and Toy Blast around 37%. Even that number is small next to what the crew called "the real games": Coin Master, Gardenscapes, Homescapes and Candy Crush, all likely north of $10B each. Which is exactly the point. You did not have to win the biggest category to build one of the best businesses in mobile puzzle. You had to pick a category nobody was defending.
Comparison of Top Blast games from January 2015 to July 2026
The obvious follow-up question is: why hasn’tanynobody done to bubble shooters what Toy Blast did to clickers? That was a genuinely large market, and it has been left alone for a decade. If you're scoping something new, the transferable lesson isn't "what's the next Super Light Ball," it's "which category is everyone currently writing off."
Jan 1, 2014 - Oct 1, 2023 Top Blast Games by Downloads
This is exactly what we see in the current market too. What people didn’t pay attention before are the ones evolving today. The easiest example would be the color sort genre and what Grand Games did.
Super Light Ball - one feature to save them all
Toon Blast ran flat, then declined, for years. Revenue went from $223.4M in H1 2021 to $188.3M in H1 2022, then dropped harder to $135M in H1 2023. That's a game visibly on its way out.
Then it wasn't. The turnaround started in October 2023, peaked at $37.6M in January 2024, and stabilised above $35M per month, more than double 2023's $16.6M monthly average. H1 2024 came in at $212.7M, back to mid-pandemic levels.
The trigger was Super Light Ball, the feature Royal Match popularised in summer 2023, where the color-clearing special item gets doubled once you unlock it, and doubles the effect of anything you combine it with. Toon Blast adapted it in roughly three months. For scale on how fast that is: Candy Crush still runs a heavily diluted version you can only use once every few levels.
So why does a generosity feature make money? Because it isn't a generosity feature, it's difficulty headroom wearing a costume. You earn Super Light Ball by winning, so once it's charged, losing a level costs you something you already own, and loss aversion converts harder than progress.
It also changes the math at the out-of-moves prompt, where casual puzzle monetisation actually lives: with a doubled board-clearer sitting there, five extra moves stop feeling like a gamble and start feeling like a closing move. And a stronger top-end tool lets you push level difficulty up without wrecking completion rates. More fails, more purchase moments, and the player experiences all of it as getting more powerful rather than getting squeezed.
Nothing competes for attention when the big clear fires, so it becomes the moment of the session, and moments players want to reproduce are the ones they'll pay to protect.
Royal Match Super Light Ball vs Toon Blast Magic Disco
The ARPDAU move is the number that made the panel stop. US ARPDAU sat somewhere around 17 to 38 cents for years, and the post-Super Light Ball figures land in the $2 to $3 range. That holds on iOS and Android separately, so it isn't a mix artifact, and it isn't a download story either. Downloads are down more than 90% from peak while revenue sits near record highs, which means the growth is coming entirely from monetising and retaining the base that stayed. Same install base, roughly 10x the value per user.
There's a nice symmetry underneath all of this. Dream Games was founded by former Peak Product Director Soner Aydemir with four ex-Peak colleagues, all of whom worked on Toy Blast and Toon Blast. So the feature that saved Toon Blast was invented by the people who built Toon Blast, at the company they left to start. The current team recognised it, moved on it in a quarter, and got a bigger lift out of it than the game it came from.
That speed is the underrated bit. Three months is not enough time to fully understand what doubling your strongest special item does to level funnel, win rate curves and economy balance. Most teams would have spent that window edge-casing it.
Peak shipped and fixed after. And the effect is more pronounced in blast than in Match-3 precisely because the board is static and low-strategy: a single high-impact clearing moment carries more weight when there's no puzzle depth competing for the player's attention. Because of the more random core, combining two Super Light Balls and clearing the whole board twice matters more in blast than the equivalent does in a switcher.
The events rebuild was the engine
Ask to split the credit for Toon Blast turnaround, and it’d land at roughly one third Super Light Ball, two thirds “everything else”. If you had to remove one, removing the events would hurt more.
What "everything else" actually contains:
The collection meta, borrowed structurally from social casino.
Wild Journey, a progression track that pays out card packs and ends in a wildcard, which resolves the classic collection dead-end where your last few cards are mathematically unobtainable. A purchase-gated wildcard offer running alongside it.
A three-tier season pass, which, as far as the panel can tell, is a casual puzzle first, imported straight from midcore and archero-likes.
The events calendar rebuild is the least discussed and possibly most important piece. Toon Blast used to run seven isolated one-day events. Rocket Monday: creating a high number of rockets during gameplay to get rewards; First Try Tuesday: Winning x amount of levels on your first try to win rewards: one mechanic, one goal, reset every morning. Around late summer 2025, those got switched off and replaced with longer, overlapping formats closer to what Royal Match runs. Roughly the same number of events, but each running two to six days, which means goals now stack on top of each other instead of expiring nightly.
Rocket Monday & First Try Tuesday Events from Toon Blast’s one-mechanic early-stage events. The goal is to have simple mechanic events that encourage players to spend.
That's the difference between a bump and an engine. Super Light Ball is a single optimised feature with a ceiling. There isn't much left to squeeze out of it. But raising the stakes of losing a level feeds directly into the value of a collection, which feeds into a longer event, which creates more purchase moments, which makes the next stakes increase land harder. Those compound. That's how you get multiple years of re-acceleration on a shrinking install base rather than one good quarter.
There's also a small detail in the event list that says a lot about where the market went: Cannon Fest, one of Toon Blast's mini-game events, is now being cloned as a standalone premise by half the hybrid-casual puzzle space. A live-ops experiment inside a nine-year-old blast game accidentally became a genre.
Cannon Fest minigame from Toon Blast on the left, “Royal Splash: Tower Blast” game in soft launch by Moon Active on the right
Which brings me to the warning worth repeating, because I expect this to have the opposite effect on some readers: Do not build a blast game.
The last few years produced a long list of blast attempts that died quietly, and the market did not need a single one of them. But the transferable lesson isn't about blast at all. It's this: when you can't grow the audience, you grow the value of the audience you have. Toon Blast stopped being a UA story years ago and became a monetisation and live ops story instead, and that's the only reason it's still here. Features and events are the entire lever once installs stop coming.
The open question is whether Peak gets to push it. The ROAS math on a game earning this much per user looks appealing enough that someone inside should be arguing for 10x the UA spend. Whether that argument survives the trip up to Take-Two and back down is a different kind of problem than a product one.
WW RPD comparison between Toon Blast, Royal Match and Royal Kingdom
Now let’s compare that with US RPD, and you’ll see the huge difference.
US RPD comparison between Toon Blast, Royal Match and Royal Kingdom
The thing I keep coming back to is that none of this was a new game.
Toon Blast is nine years old, its downloads are a tenth of what they were, and it is earning more per user than it did at its peak. Nobody rebooted it, nobody rebranded it, nobody shipped a sequel. A team just looked at a shrinking, aging, deeply committed player base and decided it was an asset rather than a problem, then spent two years testing into it.
That's a less exciting story than a breakout launch, and it's a far more repeatable one. Most studios in this market already have a Toon Blast sitting in their portfolio. They're just calling it a legacy title and quietly moving their best people off it.

  • A three-tier season pass, which, as far as the panel can tell, is a casual puzzle first, imported straight from midcore and archero-likes.

The events calendar rebuild is the least discussed and possibly most important piece. Toon Blast used to run seven isolated one-day events. Rocket Monday: creating a high number of rockets during gameplay to get rewards; First Try Tuesday: Winning x amount of levels on your first try to win rewards: one mechanic, one goal, reset every morning. Around late summer 2025, those got switched off and replaced with longer, overlapping formats closer to what Royal Match runs. Roughly the same number of events, but each running two to six days, which means goals now stack on top of each other instead of expiring nightly.

That's the difference between a bump and an engine. Super Light Ball is a single optimised feature with a ceiling. There isn't much left to squeeze out of it. But raising the stakes of losing a level feeds directly into the value of a collection, which feeds into a longer event, which creates more purchase moments, which makes the next stakes increase land harder. Those compound. That's how you get multiple years of re-acceleration on a shrinking install base rather than one good quarter.

There's also a small detail in the event list that says a lot about where the market went: Cannon Fest, one of Toon Blast's mini-game events, is now being cloned as a standalone premise by half the hybrid-casual puzzle space. A live-ops experiment inside a nine-year-old blast game accidentally became a genre.

Which brings me to the warning worth repeating, because I expect this to have the opposite effect on some readers: Do not build a blast game.

The last few years produced a long list of blast attempts that died quietly, and the market did not need a single one of them. But the transferable lesson isn't about blast at all. It's this: when you can't grow the audience, you grow the value of the audience you have. Toon Blast stopped being a UA story years ago and became a monetisation and live ops story instead, and that's the only reason it's still here. Features and events are the entire lever once installs stop coming.

The open question is whether Peak gets to push it. The ROAS math on a game earning this much per user looks appealing enough that someone inside should be arguing for 10x the UA spend. Whether that argument survives the trip up to Take-Two and back down is a different kind of problem than a product one.

Now let’s compare that with US RPD, and you’ll see the huge difference.

The thing I keep coming back to is that none of this was a new game. 

Toon Blast is nine years old, its downloads are a tenth of what they were, and it is earning more per user than it did at its peak. Nobody rebooted it, nobody rebranded it, nobody shipped a sequel. A team just looked at a shrinking, aging, deeply committed player base and decided it was an asset rather than a problem, then spent two years testing into it. 

That's a less exciting story than a breakout launch, and it's a far more repeatable one. Most studios in this market already have a Toon Blast sitting in their portfolio. They're just calling it a legacy title and quietly moving their best people off it.
